claims.text: The alloy's initial state is a single-phase solid solution.
The proposed intervention includes controlling impurities.
The proposed intervention includes optimizing alloy composition.
Controlling impurities can help maintain solid-solution strengthening during thermal exposure.
Optimizing composition can help maintain solid-solution strengthening during thermal exposure.
Maintaining solid-solution strengthening will preserve toughness after thermal exposure and subsequent loading.
The applicable thermal exposure temperature is 700°C.
The thermal exposure is followed by mechanical loading.
Thermal exposure at 700°C can produce mechanical degradation through impurity-associated phase segregation and loss of solute strengthening.
The intervention will improve toughness relative to the same alloy tested under identical conditions without the intervention.
The intervention will improve resistance to degradation relative to the untreated comparator.
Solid-solution-related lattice friction and dislocation-mediated plasticity can contribute to a favorable strength–ductility combination.
The hypothesis applies within unspecified composition and processing-condition boundaries.
Failure of the intervened alloy to improve toughness and degradation resistance relative to the control would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: Composition optimization changes the alloy composition, whereas the baseline is described as the same alloy without the intervention. The comparator is therefore internally ambiguous unless 'same alloy' means the same alloy family rather than the identical composition.
